```
Updatable doc-values

Updatable doc-values lets a `doc_values: { updatable: true }` field be changed in place with `IndexWriter.updateDocValues` instead of reindexing the whole document, on columnar indices. The first version landed in #157749, behind the `doc_values_updatable` feature flag.

Remaining work:

`RepositoryData` writes can proceed even after failure

Today `BlobStoreRepository#writeIndexGen` verifies that the `RepositoryData` generation is as expected, but this is not sufficient to prove that a different master hasn't invalidated the write it's about to do. For instance:

1. A snapshot delete starts running on master $A$ but stalls in its first interactions with the repository.
2. $A$ fails over to new master $B$.
3. $B$ restarts the delete but encounters an I/O error and drops the delete from the cluster state without updating `RepositoryData`.
4. $B$ starts running other repository operations, maybe creating new `indices/${UUID}` paths.
5. $B$ fails over back to original master $A$ before it reaches finalization for the new snapshots.
6. The stalled delete on $A$ comes back to life and lists the repository contents.
7. $A$ then updates the `RepositoryData`, which still has the expected generation.
8. $A$ then deletes any unknown `indices/${UUID}` paths it encountered, which includes any new ones that $B$'s new snapshot started to write, corrupting the repository.

The update to the pending generation needs to check that the write task still has authority to proceed: in the case of a delete, this means checking that a deletion with the given ID is still in the cluster state. A similar problem applies to snapshot creations.

Ingest: avoid document parse/serialize round-trip when a pipeline makes no changes

Every document that goes through an ingest pipeline is parsed into a `Map` and serialized back out around the pipeline execution, even when the pipeline ends up making no changes to the document. For the built-in `logs@default-pipeline`, which only sets `@timestamp` if it's missing, this means paying the full parse/serialize cost on every document that already carries a timestamp, which in practice is normally all of them.

A no-op pipeline shouldn't cost anything close to what a real one does. We should detect, cheaply, whether a given pipeline execution would be a no-op for a given document and skip the parse/serialize round-trip in that case. At minimum, special-case the `set` processor's "only if absent" behavior so `logs@default-pipeline` can skip work when `@timestamp` is already present. It's also worth checking whether this generalizes to other default pipelines and processors without reintroducing the cost it's meant to avoid.

`RestoreService` need not wait for reroute completion

If the user starts a snapshot restore with `?wait_for_completion=true` then we wait for the shards all to be assigned, which implies that the relevant reroutes have definitely completed, so there's no need for `RestoreSnapshotStateTask` to subscribe its listener to the reroute completion. On the other hand if the user starts the restore with `?wait_for_completion=false` then we can return as soon as the restore exists in the cluster state even if the corresponding reroute hasn't completed.

We should drop the `AllocationActionListener` in `RestoreSnapshotStateTask` and instead use `rerouteCompletionIsNotRequired()` to ignore the outcome of the reroute. Completing this task's listener sooner removes the possibility for `RestoreSnapshotResponse#restoreInfo` to be `null` without either `?wait_for_completion=false` or a master failover.

ES|QL: make groupability a property of the data type

Which column types can be a grouping/dedup key is encoded in four independent hard-coded lists:

- `Aggregate.checkUnsupportedGroupingType` (`x-pack/plugin/esql/src/main/java/org/elasticsearch/xpack/esql/plan/logical/Aggregate.java`) rejects `aggregate_metric_double`, `date_period`, `date_range`, `exponential_histogram`, `partial_agg`, `tdigest` and `time_duration`, and counters only when the grouping is a direct `FieldAttribute`, so a RENAMEd counter slips through (#163024). Used by STATS, INLINE STATS, LIMIT BY and DEDUP.
- `Aggregate.checkUnsupportedStatsGroupingType` (same file) additionally rejects `dense_vector`, for STATS and INLINE STATS only.
- `Dedup.surrogate()` (`.../plan/logical/Dedup.java`) keeps its own list of attributes it skips instead of deduping on.
- `Join.UNSUPPORTED_TYPES` (`.../plan/logical/join/Join.java`) lists 27 types a LOOKUP JOIN key cannot have.

Every new data type needs a separate decision in each list, and the lists drift. Recent examples: union-typed columns (#164589), counters reached via RENAME (#163024), `_unmapped_fields` (#166773).

This story makes groupability a declared property of the type: a `groupable` flag on the `DataType` builder (default false, so a forgotten decision rejects instead of corrupting results), exposed as `DataType.isGroupable()` and set per type to match today's verifier behavior. `checkUnsupportedGroupingType` collapses to `isGroupable() == false`. The rejection message tells the user to convert or drop the column, and DEDUP's variant names DEDUP instead of "group by". Two deliberate choices:

- Counters are groupable. A renamed counter is accepted today and groups correctly at runtime (counter blocks use the same element type as their base type, so they hash identically), which makes rejecting only the direct field a loophole rather than a policy. Counter columns become legal grouping keys everywhere.
- `dense_vector` stays rejected in STATS and INLINE STATS as a command-level exception (`BlockHash` has no dense_vector grouping support), but is groupable, since LIMIT BY and DEDUP group it.

The property carries an equality contract:

- The groupable set only grows, and existing groupable types keep today's grouping behavior (LIMIT BY is already GA). A new type is groupable only if its grouping matches the type's own `==` semantics from day one.
- GA protects the contract, not accidents. Where an existing key disagrees with the type's own `==` by accident — e.g. `0.0` and `-0.0` landing in different groups — that is a bug, fixed in its own PR with a release note. What stays is what was decided: null equality, list semantics, spatial shapes compared as bytes.
- For multivalued fields, whether values arrive ordered or sorted is a property of the field (a columnar source keeps insertion order, doc values sort), so the field type declares it and each field's values compare as its type defines. ES|QL adds no rules of its own linking `_source` and doc values.
- A container type defines its own equality: `_unmapped_fields` compares like a flattened field — keys and values regardless of order — not as JSON text.

Enforcement so the lists cannot drift again:

- a verifier matrix test iterating `DataType.values()`, asserting for each type that the STATS BY, INLINE STATS BY, LIMIT 1 BY and DEDUP outcome matches `isGroupable()`;
- an engine-invariant test asserting every groupable type can build a grouping over its element type, so the property never claims comparability the engine cannot deliver. #166812 moves LIMIT BY/DEDUP grouping from `GroupKeyEncoder` to `BlockHash` with no change in behavior, so the encoding checks target the direct encoders.

`Join.UNSUPPORTED_TYPES` is a follow-up: it rejects several groupable types (`text`, `version`, `unsigned_long`, spatial types) for join-specific reasons, so it cannot collapse to `isGroupable()` alone.

Get component templates: return only templates valid for a given index mode

Add a parameter to `GET _component_template` that takes an index mode and returns only the component templates that would pass validation in an index template using that mode. The first use is `columnar` and `logsdb_columnar`.

Kibana is adding `columnar` and `logsdb_columnar` to the index template wizard. After a user picks one of these modes, the component templates step still lists every component template, including ones whose mappings or settings columnar rejects, such as mapping-level runtime fields or `doc_values: false`.

Elasticsearch already rejects these compositions when the index template is saved. In Kibana, the user finds out at the last step of the wizard, from an error about fields defined in a component template they may not own. A filter lets the picker list only templates that will work, and keeps the compatibility rules in Elasticsearch.

Agreed in principle with @martijnvg.

- A query parameter on `GET _component_template` that takes an index mode. Naming is up to Storage Engine.
- A template is excluded only if it would fail the same validation that runs when an index template using that mode is saved.
- Setting `index.mode` doesn't exclude a template on its own. The index template's `index.mode` takes precedence, so the composition is valid.

Kibana can work with the filter alone: it hides excluded templates and tells the user the list is filtered by index mode. If it's cheap to add, a variant that returns every template with a compatibility flag and a reason (for example, the rejected field and option) would let Kibana show incompatible templates as disabled with an explanation. Nice to have, not required.

Kibana Index Management: the component templates step of the index template wizard, when the index mode is `columnar` or `logsdb_columnar`.

Stale refresh-block timer can unblock a recreated index early

The expiry mechanism in `RemoveRefreshClusterBlockService` only uses the name of the target index in the removal task and ignores its UUID:

https://github.com/elastic/elasticsearch/blob/ea78de7c4512198586456ee483438d972a9ee6ad/x-pack/plugin/stateless/src/main/java/org/elasticsearch/xpack/stateless/recovery/RemoveRefreshClusterBlockService.java#L361-L368

When an refresh-blocked index is deleted, its refresh-block expiry timer carries on running. Users could then create a new index under the same name such that when the refresh-block expiry timer triggers it inappropriately removes a refresh block from the new and independently refresh-blocked index.

Delayed refresh-block removal for zero-replica indices on master failover

`RemoveRefreshClusterBlockService` skips the zero-replica check on master election. A master may perform the replica-count update but then stand down before removing the refresh block. The next master starts a new expiration timer but does not check for indices in this intermediate state which need immediate processing. With only `INDEX_ONLY` primaries remaining, search readiness also cannot trigger removal, so the block can persist until another metadata update or the expiration timer fires.

Applies in `3fd646162fbdee7ebeb88c0f565503c05b79e244` but it's been like that for a while.
```

```
Cleanup of `RepositoryCleanupInProgress` may drop active cleanup on master failover

`TransportCleanupRepositoryAction#removeInProgressCleanup` clears whichever `RepositoryCleanupInProgress` entry is present. If a master steps down during a cleanup, the new master clears the entry on failover, but the original cleanup’s completion callback can still be pending on the old master.

If the old master is re-elected and starts another cleanup before that callback runs, the stale `remove repository cleanup task` clears the new cleanup’s entry. This allows snapshot operations to start while the new cleanup is still running. If a snapshot creation running alongside such an orphaned cleanup encounters a new index then it will create objects in a new `indices/${UUID}` path which the orphaned cleanup might then delete. The orphaned cleanup might also write a higher-generation `RepositoryData` object than the concurrent snapshot creations/deletions, reverting changes made by those intervening operations.
```

```
ES|QL `unmapped_fields="load"` is quadratic in the number of named fields on synthetic-source indices - With `SET unmapped_fields="load"` on a synthetic-source index, query cost grows roughly with the **square** of the number of unmapped fields named. With stored source it grows linearly. - Example: 2,000 documents, 998 keyword fields each, 100 mapped. Naming all 898 unmapped fields takes about 110 s on synthetic source and under 1 s on stored. - `LOAD_ALL` is about 2x slower on synthetic source. Queries over mapped fields only are unaffected. - Cause: the synthetic source loader compiles a source filter once per ignored value, per document. Caching it removes the slowdown (see the experiment below). I first saw this in Rally (`esql_unmapped_fields`, 1M documents), where `load` went from about 0.4 s to about 20 s. - Single node, `9.7.0-SNAPSHOT` (build `1fde6444`), trial licence (without one, synthetic source falls back to stored). - Each document has `field_0` to `field_997`, random 12-character strings. The index is `dynamic: false`, with the first M fields mapped as `keyword`, 1 shard, force-merged to one segment. - `index.mapping.source.mode` is `stored` or `synthetic`. - The query names every unmapped field. Timings are the median of 7 runs after 3 warmups, in ms, `LIMIT 1000`: ``` SET unmapped_fields="load"; FROM idx | KEEP field_M, ..., field_997 | LIMIT 1000 ``` Repro script (Python 3, standard library only) ``` """Repro: ES|QL unmapped_fields="load" on stored vs synthetic source. Each doc has 998 keyword-valued fields. The index is dynamic:false and maps the first M of them. Query names every unmapped field (field_M .. field_997), LIMIT 1000. """ import json import random import statistics import string import sys [... 104 more lines] ``` **Naming every unmapped field** | Mapped / unmapped | Stored | Synthetic | Ratio | |---|---|---|---| | 100 / 898 | 803 | 106,732 | 133x | | 499 / 499 | 470 | 55,755 | 119x | | 898 / 100 | 157 | 1,386 | 9x | **100 mapped, varying how many unmapped fields are named** | Named | Stored | Synthetic | Ratio | |---|---|---|---| | 1 | 106 | 155 | 1.5x | | 50 | 129 | 437 | 3.4x | | 100 | 148 | 1,516 | 10x | | 200 | 202 | 5,787 | 29x | | 400 | 323 | 22,769 | 70x | | 500 | 495 | 53,108 | 107x | | 898 | 890 | 111,389 | 125x | - Doubling from 100 to 200 and from 200 to 400 named fields costs 3.9x each time, which is quadratic. Past about 500 it grows more slowly (2.1x for 500 to 898). - The cost depends on how many fields are named, not on how many unmapped fields the document has: with 100 named, a document with 100 unmapped fields took 1.4 s and one with 898 took 1.5 s. **`default` and `LOAD_ALL`** | Mapped | `default` stored / synthetic | `LOAD_ALL` stored / synthetic | |---|---|---| | 100 | 39 / 36 | 313 / 665 (2.1x) | | 499 | 239 / 236 | 511 / 926 (1.8x) | | 898 | 416 / 413 | 549 / 855 (1.6x) | Six `jcmd Thread.print` samples during the slowest query. Excluding idle selector threads, 6 of the 12 busy search or ES|QL samples had this stack: ``` UnmappedFields.walk BlockLoaderStoredFieldsFromLeafLoader.source SourceLoader$Synthetic$SyntheticLeaf.source / write ObjectMapper$SyntheticSourceFieldLoader.prepare FieldWriter$IgnoredSource. XContentParserConfigurationImpl.withFiltering FilterPath.compile ``` In `SyntheticSourceFieldLoader.prepare` (`ObjectMapper.java`, read at `c513e1f268b5`), each ignored-source value of the document gets a new `FieldWriter.IgnoredSource(filter, value)`. Its constructor calls `withFiltering(...)`, which compiles a new `FilterPath` over all include paths. ES|QL restricts the source to the N named fields, so each document does about N compiles of an N-path filter. I cached the `XContentParserConfiguration` per `(SourceFilter, field name)` in `IgnoredSource` (a static unbounded map: fine for an experiment, not for production; `SourceFilter` has identity equality). The stored column is a range across the two runs. - Result sets for `load` naming 50 and 300 fields, on stored and synthetic, baseline and patched: all eight hashes identical. XContentParserConfiguration.EMPTY : EXPERIMENT_CACHE.computeIfAbsent( new ExperimentCacheKey(filter, initialValue.name()), k -> XContentParserConfiguration.EMPTY.withFiltering( initialValue.name(), [... 6 more lines] ``` A real fix would keep the compiled configuration with the loader (per source filter and field, for the loader's lifetime) instead of a static map. Generic ignore_malformed handling for columnar batch mapping

Follow-up from https://github.com/elastic/elasticsearch/pull/163924#discussion_r4628998756

On the columnar batch path, a mapper that hits a malformed value with `ignore_malformed: true`
either throws `UnsupportedOperationException` (falling the whole chunk back to the row path,
e.g. `HistogramFieldMapper` in #163924), or re-implements the row-path behaviour itself.
#165648 did the latter for `IpFieldMapper` (`MalformedCapture`, `batchCanStoreMalformed`):
it adds the field to `_ignored` via `BatchMappingContext#addIgnoredFieldColumnar` and,
for synthetic source, writes the malformed value to the `._ignore_malformed` / `._on_failure`
sidecar columns with the right encoding and index-version gating.

None of that logic is specific to IP fields. Copying it into every mapper that gains batch
support (histogram, numbers, dates, ...) duplicates subtle encoding/version rules and
risks divergence from the row path.

Add a utility on `BatchMappingContext` (or a helper it hands out) that, given a field and a
row, applies `ignore_malformed: true` the same way the row path does:
- report the field in `_ignored` once per document;
- depending on source mode / index version, encode and store the original value in the
  appropriate sidecar column (`_ignored_source`, `._ignore_malformed`, `._on_failure`);
- expose whether the current index layout supports this on the batch path, so mappers only
  fall back when it does not.

Then migrate `IpFieldMapper` to it and use it from `HistogramFieldMapper` instead of
falling back on malformed rows.

`ignore_malformed: false` (rejecting individual documents) needs per-row failure marking
and error reporting in the batch indexer, and is tracked separately.

Investigate the overhead of kNN query sampling on the search path when always on

The kNN query sampling plugin (#160582) captures a share of kNN searches on the coordinating node and passes them to one background thread that deduplicates and samples them. The capture runs on every eligible kNN search once sampling is enabled. A concern was raised that keeping sampling always on could noticeably affect search performance and that the pipeline is more complex than it needs to be.

We do not yet have a view on where the cost sits or how large it is. This issue is to find that out and decide whether anything has to change.

- What does sampling cost per search, in throughput, latency (p50, p99, p99.9) and CPU, with it off, at the default capture rate, and with every search captured?
- Which part of the pipeline accounts for the cost: the capture on the search thread, the hand-off to the background thread, or the work on the background thread (fingerprint, tracker, strata, sampler)?
- How does the cost change with the type of traffic (repeated queries or mostly new queries), the number of dimensions, `k`, and the size of the index (search time)?
- Does the cost depend on the settings, such as the capture rate, the capture floor and the strata?
- Is the bound of one background thread enough to protect the node under the highest traffic, and what happens when the queue is full?

- Microbenchmarks (JMH) for each stage, with the GC and CPU profilers.
- An end-to-end run on a node under load with sampling off, at the default capture rate, and capturing every search, and a CPU profile (flame graph) of the node in each mode.
- Repeat on a larger index, where a search takes longer, and with different vector sizes.

A short write-up with the numbers and the profiles, and, if the cost is not negligible, proposals to reduce it, each with its trade-offs.

Related: #160582, #160497
```

```
`MlDailyMaintenanceService` starts to double-trigger tasks on master failover

If `MlDailyMaintenanceService#stop` is called while `triggerTasks()` is running, the `ScheduledCancellableAdapter#scheduledFuture` within `cancellable` is already complete, so cancelling it does nothing. `triggerTasks()` then calls `scheduleNext()` from `finally`. `start()` also calls `scheduleNext()` and does not cancel the previous future. A `stop()`/`start()` pair before that `finally`, or a later `start()` after `finally` has already installed the next run, therefore leaves two scheduled tasks. Each `triggerTasks()` schedules its own successor, and later calls to `stop()` only cancel the future currently referenced by `cancellable`, so the extra chain keeps triggering maintenance.

Essentially the same bug as https://github.com/elastic/elasticsearch/issues/166738 (cancelling a completed future does nothing) but with the opposite effect.

`EnrichPolicyMaintenanceService` gets stuck on master failover

If `EnrichPolicyMaintenanceService#offMaster` is called while the service is running `cleanUpEnrichIndices()` then the `ScheduledCancellableAdapter#scheduledFuture` within `cancellable` is already complete, so cancelling it does nothing. The cleanup thread then calls `scheduleNext()` but the `isMaster` check fails so this does not replace `cancellable`. A later call to `EnrichPolicyMaintenanceService#onMaster` sees a non-null `cancellable` which is not cancelled, and therefore does not call `scheduleNext()` to schedule the next execution. Moreover, later calls to `offMaster` do not clear this state, so this node will never again schedule a cleanup.

Applies at `11849f0b05bbf47f2947330bd84ca540326e4e4e` (current `main`) but it's been like this for ages.
```

```
ESQL: LOOKUP JOIN and ENRICH don't bring in keys of flattened fields

A lookup index never contributes the keys of its `flattened` fields, while a `FROM` index does. After `FROM flattened_paths_mapped | LOOKUP JOIN flattened_paths_lookup ON id`, `attributes.host` keeps the main index's value and `attributes.zone` is null even when the lookup row has it. #165400 currently locks this in (`keywordWithLookupJoin`, `keyWithLookupJoin`, `keyOnlyTheLookupIndexHolds`).

`ENRICH` is the same case. The policy runner copies each enrich field's mapping type from the source index, so an enrich field can be `flattened`. No ES|QL test covers that yet. `WITH` can name only enrich fields, not their keys.

**Rule** (proposed by Jim Ferenczi): a key is a column like any other name. `attributes` and `attributes.host` are two columns, like `country` and `country.keyword`. A command replaces only the exact names it brings in. A name refers to an existing column of that name, and otherwise to the key of its flattened parent, added as a new column. This is backwards compatible and needs no setting.

**Exception:** `DROP attributes.host` removes the column and also the `host` key inside `attributes`. Open question: should only `DROP`/`KEEP` patterns reach into flattened fields?

[ML] Failed anomaly detection job waits for a lazy ML node that autoscaling never provides

main (seen on serverless, 9.7.0-SNAPSHOT)

A `failed` anomaly detection job does not recover on its own; it must be force-closed and reopened. That is fine. The problem is that after its ML node scales away, the failed job asks for a lazy node that autoscaling never provides. Its audit messages then say it is a memory problem, and they repeat every 30 minutes for as long as nobody force-closes the job.

Observed sequence after an `autodetect` crash (SIGSEGV):

1. Job goes to `failed`. Datafeed fails to post data and stops.
2. ML tier scales to 0, because `MlAutoscalingContext.taskStateFilter` excludes `FAILED` jobs, so no job holds the node.
3. The job's persistent task becomes unassigned: audit `Job relocating.`
4. `OpenJobPersistentTasksExecutor.doGetAssignment` does not check the job state. `JobNodeSelector.considerLazyAssignment` returns `AWAITING_LAZY_ASSIGNMENT` because there are 0 ML nodes and lazy nodes are allowed.
5. `auditRequireMemoryIfNecessary` writes `Job requires at least [40.9mb] free memory on a machine learning node to run; [0b] are available. The current total capacity for ML [total: 0b, largest node: 0b].`
6. Autoscaling ignores the task: `MlAutoscalingContext.anomalyDetectionTasks` drops `FAILED` jobs, and both `MlAutoscalingResourceTracker` (serverless) and `MlMemoryAutoscalingDecider` read that list. `minNodes` stays 0 and no ML node arrives.
7. `auditedJobCapacity` has `expireAfterWrite(30m)`, so step 5 repeats every 30 minutes.

Even if an ML node did join, `OpenJobPersistentTasksExecutor.nodeOperation` returns early for `FAILED`, so assignment cannot help.

Result for the user: job stats show `state: failed` with `assignment_explanation: persistent task is awaiting node assignment.`, and the audit trail is full of capacity messages. These point to a sizing problem, while the real cause is the earlier process failure. Operator runbooks that treat "awaiting node assignment for more than 30 minutes" as insufficient memory give the wrong diagnosis.

Relevant code:

- `x-pack/plugin/ml/src/main/java/org/elasticsearch/xpack/ml/autoscaling/MlAutoscalingContext.java`: `taskStateFilter(JobState)` excludes `CLOSED` and `FAILED`.
- `x-pack/plugin/ml/src/main/java/org/elasticsearch/xpack/ml/job/task/OpenJobPersistentTasksExecutor.java`: `doGetAssignment` (no state check), `nodeOperation` (early return for `FAILED`).
- `x-pack/plugin/ml/src/main/java/org/elasticsearch/xpack/ml/task/AbstractJobPersistentTasksExecutor.java`: `auditedJobCapacity` TTL cache and `auditRequireMemoryIfNecessary`.
- `x-pack/plugin/ml/src/main/java/org/elasticsearch/xpack/ml/job/JobNodeSelector.java`: `considerLazyAssignment`.

Possible fix: when the job task state is `FAILED`, return a non-lazy assignment with an explanation such as `job is in the failed state. Force close and reopen the job.`, and do not write the capacity audit. This makes assignment consistent with the autoscaler, which already ignores failed jobs. The same check is worth applying to data frame analytics and snapshot upgrade tasks, which have matching `FAILED` filters in `MlAutoscalingContext`.

1. On a cluster with ML autoscaling (or serverless), open an anomaly detection job with a datafeed.
2. Kill the `autodetect` process (`kill -SEGV <pid>`) so that the job goes to `failed`.
3. Wait for ML autoscaling to remove the ML node.
4. `GET _ml/anomaly_detectors/<job>/_stats`: `state: failed`, `assignment_explanation: persistent task is awaiting node assignment.`
5. Check the job audit messages: `Job requires at least [...] free memory ...; [0b] are available` every ~30 minutes. No ML node is added.
```

    | EVAL languages = "english"
    | WHERE emp_no IN (FROM employees | WHERE salary > 50000 | KEEP emp_no)
```

is equivalent to:

```
  FROM employees
    | WHERE emp_no IN (FROM employees | WHERE salary > 40000 | KEEP emp_no)
    | WHERE emp_no IN (FROM employees | WHERE salary > 50000 | KEEP emp_no)
    | EVAL languages = "english"
```

but right now it doesn't get rewritten to that second version in logical planning, because the IN filter turns into a `SemiJoin` in view / subquery resolution and `PushDownAndCombineFilters` cannot pick it up.
```

```
ES|QL: Second cast of a union-typed field after LOOKUP JOIN creates a duplicate converted field

When a union-typed field is cast, then a `LOOKUP JOIN` follows, and the same field is cast again, the analyzer creates a second synthetic converted field instead of reusing the first. The analyzed plan then has two `$$<field>$converted_to$<type>` attributes with the same name, and `PlanConsistencyChecker` reports "duplicate output attribute".

Found while reviewing #166364. It reproduces on `main` without that PR, so it is not caused by it.

`id` is `keyword` in `union_index_1` and `integer` in `union_index_2`; `languages_lookup` is a lookup index.

```
FROM union_index*
| EVAL a = id::keyword
| EVAL language_code = 1
| LOOKUP JOIN languages_lookup ON language_code
| EVAL b = id::keyword
```

Analyze the query, then run `PlanConsistencyChecker.checkPlan` on every node. It fails with:

```
Plan [EsRelation[union_index*]...[!id, name{f}#13, $$id$converted_to$keyword{f$}#16, ..]] optimized incorrectly due to duplicate output attribute $$id$converted_to$keyword{f$}#17
Plan [Eval[[$$id$converted_to$keyword{f$}#16 AS a#5]]] optimized incorrectly due to duplicate output attribute $$id$converted_to$keyword{f$}#17
Plan [Eval[[1[INTEGER] AS language_code#7]]] optimized incorrectly due to duplicate output attribute $$id$converted_to$keyword{f$}#17
```

The first cast creates field #16 and the second creates #17, both named `$$id$converted_to$keyword`. Without the `LOOKUP JOIN` between the casts the second cast reuses the first field.

The query from the review comment (https://github.com/elastic/elasticsearch/pull/166364#discussion_r4621048421) uses `sample_data, sample_data_ts_long` with `message_types_lookup`. I have not run it end to end, so I do not know whether it fails in a real query or only fails the plan consistency check.

Not investigated. The lookup side is not the cause: it holds no converted field. Something in the reuse lookup (`createIfDoesNotAlreadyExist` / the per-scope `unionFieldAttributes` state in `ResolveUnionTypes`) appears not to see the first field once the plan contains the join.
```

```
ESQL: push WHERE filters down into the EQL source command

ES|QL pushes a `WHERE` on a `FROM` source down to the index search. `PushDownAndCombineFilters` moves it through `RENAME`/`EVAL` aliases, `PushDownFilterAndLimitIntoUnionAll` moves it into view and subquery branches, and `PushFiltersToSource` turns it into the Lucene query. A request `filter` on a view becomes a `WHERE` on the view's output (#165612) and follows the same path. The EQL source command has no quivalent: only `PushLimitIntoEqlRelation`, for `LIMIT`. Its `EqlSearchRequest` already has a `filter` field, which #166313 uses for the request filter on EQL sources outside views.

A `WHERE` after an EQL source runs on what the EQL search returned: at most the result-truncation limit of events, by default the most recent ones. The `WHERE` also keeps a `LIMIT` from reaching the command. A filter on an older time window can therefore return fewer rows than exist, or none, with only the truncation warning. This affects:
  - views: `FROM eql_view` with a request `filter`, or `FROM eql_view | WHERE …`.
  - regular queries: `EQL logs-* "process where true" | WHERE @timestamp < "…"`.

We should look into how feasible it is to add a logical optimizer rule, next to `PushLimitIntoEqlRelation`, that moves a `Filter` directly above an `EqlRelation` into the EQL search's `filter`. The existing rules already bring the `Filter` there. Conjuncts that can't be pushed stay above the source.
This will probably be valid **only for event queries**. For `sequence` and `sample`, filtering before matching changes which events pair up, including `until` and `![…]` missing events. Also exclude queries with `head`/`tail` pipes or a `size` option.

Also, the EQL `filter` is plain Query DSL, run in an ordinary search context. ES|QL's `SingleValueQuery`, which gives multi-valued fields ES|QL's semantics, requires `EsqlSearchExecutionContext` and fails there. Without it, Lucene's any-value matching gives different results on multi-valued fields. We need a translation that works in a plain search, or we limit pushdown to conditions where this can't happen.

segmentSortedByDescTimestamp ignores the index sort's multi-value mode

`LongValuesComparatorSource.segmentSortedByDescTimestamp` (introduced in #141755, "Speed up MatchAll queries sorted by the reverse of the index sort") decides that a segment is sorted by descending `@timestamp` from the segment's `SortField` reverse flag and missing value only. It does not look at the sort's multi-value mode (`SortedNumericSelector.Type`, i.e. `min` or `max`).

For a multi-valued `@timestamp`, the segment order depends on which value the index sort picked per document. A query sorting on `@timestamp` with a different selector than the index sort can then be treated as "the reverse of the index sort" even though the document order differs, so the early-termination / tail-collection optimisation may return wrong top hits.

A regular index, not data-stream specific:

```
index.sort.field: @timestamp
index.sort.order: desc
index.sort.mode: min        # the mode differs from the default `max` for desc
```

Index documents where `@timestamp` is multi-valued, then run a match-all query sorted on `@timestamp` in the direction that the optimisation treats as the reverse of the index sort, with a selector that disagrees with the index sort's mode. Compare hits with and without the optimisation.

`segmentSortedByDescTimestamp` should only return `true` when the index sort's multi-value mode is compatible with the query's sort (for the descending case, `max`), or the field is single-valued in the segment.

Found while reviewing #163447 (`index.sort` expression setting, which allows `MV_MIN(@timestamp) DESC` and so makes the mode easier to set). The behaviour is not new there: any index with `index.sort.field: @timestamp`, `index.sort.order: desc` and a non-default `index.sort.mode` is affected. That PR only adds the missing-first case where every document has a value, so this is tracked separately.

[ML] Zone-aware planner adds allocations to deployments already allocated in another zone

8.19, 9.x, main

_bundled_

If a previously assigned deployment (one that had allocations before but has none now) doesn’t fit on any node, the zone-aware planner retries in a mode that forces allocations for previously assigned deployments. That retry also adds an allocation to deployments that are already fully allocated in another zone, so they end up with extra allocations.

This happens because zones are planned one by one, in name order. While the planner handles the first zone, it doesn’t yet count allocations in later zones, so a fully allocated deployment there looks unallocated.

Example (two zones with one node each, 4 processors per node, 1 thread per allocation):

- `m_1` requests 2 allocations and has both in zone `z2`.
- `m_2` had allocations before but has none now, and doesn’t fit on any node.
- Expected: `m_1` keeps its 2 allocations in `z2`. Actual: it gets an extra allocation in `z1`, so 3 allocations while it requested 2.

This is triggered by any idle deployment with adaptive `min_number_of_allocations: 0` that had allocations before, since it counts as a previously assigned deployment without allocations.

Add following test to `ZoneAwareAssignmentPlannerTests`:

```

     * Deployment m_1 is fully allocated in zone z2. Deployment m_2 was previously assigned but cannot be placed anymore.
     * m_1 must keep its current allocations.

        Node node2 = new Node("n_2", ByteSizeValue.ofGb(1).getBytes(), 4);

```
[ML] Assignment planner keeps more allocations than requested

8.19, 9.x, main

_bundled_

When a trained model deployment has more allocations than its `number_of_allocations`, and the ML nodes can’t satisfy every deployment, the planner keeps the surplus instead of reducing it. Those processors stay unavailable to the under-allocated deployments.

Cause: `AbstractPreserveAllocations` doesn’t cap preserved allocations at the requested number (`allocations() - calculatePreservedAllocations()` can go negative).

Repro (one node, 4 processors, 1 thread per allocation):

`m_1` requests 2 allocations and currently has 3.
`m_2` requests 4 allocations and currently has 1.
Expected: `m_1` gets 2 and `m_2` gets 2. Actual: `m_1` keeps 3.

Total demand has to exceed capacity for this to happen. If `m_2` requests only 2 (total demand 4 = capacity), the planner trims `m_1` to 2 correctly. Only when not every deployment can be satisfied does it take the “preserve all current allocations” path, which keeps the surplus. With availability zones, capacity is checked per zone, so this also happens when the cluster as a whole has enough capacity.

Note: you can get in this situation via: https://github.com/elastic/elasticsearch/issues/166496

This unit test reproduces the issue (add to `AssignmentPlannerTests`):
```
    /**
     * Deployment m_1 has more allocations than requested, while the node lacks capacity to satisfy deployment m_2.
     * The plan must reduce m_1 to the requested number of allocations instead of preserving the surplus.
     */
    public void testGivenOverAllocatedDeployment_AndInsufficientCapacity_ReducesToRequestedAllocations() {
        Node node = new Node("n_1", ByteSizeValue.ofGb(4).getBytes(), 4);
        Deployment overAllocated = new Deployment("m_1", "m_1", ByteSizeValue.ofMb(100).getBytes(), 2, 1, Map.of("n_1", 3), 3, null, 0, 0);

```
DiskBBQ merge pass 2 reads scattered temp-file data and thrashes the page cache on small nodes

Pass 2 of the DiskBBQ merge (`IVFVectorsWriter#mergeOneFieldIVF` → `buildAndWritePostingsLists`) reads the quantized vectors back from the `qvec_` temp file one at a time, cluster by cluster (`ES950DiskBBQVectorsWriter#readQuantizedVector`: `seek` + `readBytes`). A cluster's members are spread across the whole temp file, so these are scattered reads. On a small node, where the page cache is about the size of the temp file or smaller, this thrashes the cache.

What we saw on a 4 GiB pod (about 1.1 GiB of page cache) with two ~4.5 GB merges running together for about 2 hours:

- About 800 major faults per second and about 3 GB/s of disk reads, around 23 TB in total.
- Roughly 2 MB of disk reads per merged vector (about 12M vectors).
- Almost every page read was a refault: `workingset_refault_file` was about equal to the pages read.
- About 4 MB read per major fault, which looks like read-around windows. I haven't verified that.
- About 75% of the container's CPU was kernel time, and the container hit its CPU quota.
- The merge threads were the readers visible in the stacks. I haven't proven they were the only ones.

Maybe we should use random-access advice for these reads.

OTLP endpoints and _bulk handle attributes inconsistently

OTLP is very flexible in what attribute types it allows. Some of these types are currently handled inconsistently, depending on the ingest path that is being used. We should fix those.

OTLP has an explicit "binary" type, we have a [binary field type](https://www.elastic.co/docs/reference/elasticsearch/mapping-reference/binary). However, the current behaviour differes depending on how it is ingested and in which context the attribute appears:
 * via OTLP:
    * The value is converted to `XContent` using `XContentGenerator.writeBinary`: On CBOR, this preserves a hint that the written string is actually a binary value. And this hint is respected when the dynamic mapping for the attribute is first resolved, turning it into a `binary` ES field.
    * When the attribute is a metric dimension:
       * The _tsid computation in the OTLP endpoint silently ignores binary attributes, but they are still ingested
       * As a result, the field is mapped under `attributes.*` but is not a dimension (because `binary` is not supported as a dimension)
 * Via _bulk with the collector and elasticsearchexporter:
   * The collector doesn't write CBOR, but textual JSON. In textual JSON there is no hint that something is a binary, so it will be written as a string.
   * As a result, the attribute is mapped as `keyword` instead of `binary`

**Proposed solution**:
  * Add a dynamic template which can be used to explicitly ingest binary attributes as `binary`, even via _bulk
  * For metrics: Reject datapoints with binary attributes as unsupported
     * Alternative considered: We could map those as `keyword` with the base64 string instead. But this might lead to bwc trouble in the longer term and is just a workaround for the actual fix: Supporting `binary` as TSDB dimension type.

OTLP supports nested arrays as attributes, for example `["foo", ["bar", "baz"]]`.
These cause problems when used as metric dimensions:
 * when ingested via OTLP:
   * During _tsid computation in the OTLP endpoint, nested arrays are flattend: `["foo", ["bar", "baz"]]` gets the same hash as `["foo", "bar", "baz"]`
   * The ingested document carries the original nested array in the payload. The mapper then usually flattens it.
  * when ingested via _bulk:
    * The document is ingested with the nested array in the JSON payload
    * `XContentParserTsidFunnel` doesn't support nested arrays for the _tsid computation and rejects the document

**Proposed solution**:
 * Fix nested arrays in `XContentParserTsidFunnel` by treating them as flattened. Ensure that the columnar path works the same way.

Example: `my.attribute: { "foo" : "bar", "baz" : [1, 2, 3]}`

We do have a dynamic template rule in place, which maps non-scalar attributes as `flattened`. This rule is currently applied to traces, metrics and logs. For metrics this is problematic:

We don't support `flattened` as a dimension and the `XContentParserTsidFunnel` doesn't know about this mapping. `XContentParserTsidFunnel` assumes that object will be flattened and makes each leaf part of the _tsid. The OTLP endpoint _tsid computation has the same behaviour.

So the field ends up being mapped as a non-dimension, but influenced the _tsid computation.

**Proposed Solution**:
Reject metric fields with complex data points as attributes. Flattening them (!= mapping as `flattened`) would probably be not a good idea, as this leads easily to mapping explosions.

DiskBBQ vector merges can't be aborted once started

A running DiskBBQ merge doesn't react to an abort. Close, relocation and shutdown have to wait for it to finish, and on large segments (or small nodes) that takes a long time. We saw two ~4.5 GB merges run for about 2 hours.

This is the DiskBBQ version of #158407 (HNSW) and #107513 (checksums), and an instance of apache/lucene#11694. In 9.7.0 / Lucene 10.5.2:

- There are no `checkAborted` calls anywhere under `index/codec`, including `IVFVectorsWriter` and the `ES920`/`ES940`/`ES950`/`ESNext` writers. The only explicit check is Lucene's, once per input reader at the start of `KnnVectorsWriter#merge`, before any IVF work.
- The only implicit check is `RateLimitedIndexOutput` on the `ivf*` outputs, about every 1 MiB written.
- Clustering, calibration and the pass-2 reads have no checks at all.
- Relocation aborts are polled through `IndexEngine`'s `isAborted()` override (#165443), but the rate limiter reads `mergeProgress.isAborted()` directly, so it never triggers that poll.

Hot-thread dumps taken 5 seconds to 2.5 minutes into a primary relocation still show merge threads in `buildAndWritePostingsLists` and `IvfAutoCalibration`. Queued merges were aborted when the relocation started, but the running ones carried on.

We should call `mergeState.checkAborted()` during the merge process.

Related: #158407, #107513, #165443, #152342, #89821, apache/lucene#11694.

[ML] Re-evaluating every unassigned datafeed on each cluster state update saturates the master at ~5.8k ML persistent tasks

On a cluster with ~5.8k ML persistent tasks (~2.9k anomaly detection jobs + ~2.9k datafeeds) and ~14k indices, any event that makes a large share of those tasks unassigned at the same time leaves the elected master with 30–55 s cluster-state publications for many hours. Two independent triggers produced the same signature on one production cluster within a week:

1. Disabling ML upgrade mode (`POST _ml/set_upgrade_mode?enabled=false`) after a rolling plan.
2. Five of eight ML nodes dropping out of the cluster for 1–6 minutes (transport delays, no restart, no upgrade mode involved).

The master is not short of heap or CPU. The cost is a single-threaded loop on the applier thread that re-evaluates every unassigned datafeed on every cluster state update, combined with ML task-state writes that are each their own unbatched cluster state update. This issue tracks reproducing the behaviour at scale, quantifying where the time goes, and choosing between the fixes below.

Version: 8.19.19 (ECE). The relevant code is unchanged on `main` as far as I can see, so I expect 9.x to be affected too.

| | |
|---|---|
| Elasticsearch | 8.19.19 |
| Nodes | ~70 (8 ML, 3 dedicated masters, hot/warm/cold/frozen) |
| Indices / shards | ~14.2k open indices / ~32k shards |
| ML | ~3.1k jobs, ~3.1k datafeeds (~5.8k persistent tasks), real-time datafeeds |
| Datafeed sources | about half read only from remote clusters (CCS); the other half read local data streams, avg ~390 backing indices, max ~1,170 |
| `xpack.ml.node_concurrent_job_allocations` | 16 (transient) |
| Snapshots | hourly SLM snapshot of all indices |

- Upgrade mode was on for ~5.5 h during a rolling plan. No slow cluster state applier warnings appeared during that time.
- When upgrade mode was disabled, the first `ClusterApplierService ... took [30s+]` warning appeared 4 minutes later. There were no such warnings in the 9 days before.
- 811 such warnings followed on the two masters that held the role during the incident. In each warning, `PersistentTasksClusterService` accounted for ≥ 99.9 % of the time. Typical value: `took [46.4s]`, with `PersistentTasksClusterService ... took [46398ms]`.
- Hot threads on the elected master: the applier thread at 100 % CPU, 10/10 samples in
  `DatafeedNodeSelector.checkAssignment` → `verifyIndicesActive()` ← `PersistentTasksClusterService.createAssignment` ← `shouldReassignPersistentTasks` ← `clusterChanged`.
- Pending tasks peaked at ~29.5k (about 91 % `update snapshot state`, the rest mainly ILM and ML task-state updates), with the oldest task waiting ~77 min.
- Recovery without intervention: unassigned jobs 1,419 → 581 and stale datafeeds 1,545 → 709 over ~12 h (~80 per hour). The master was back to normal after roughly 30 h in total.
- Second trigger: five ML nodes were removed by the master's health checks at the same moment (transport sends delayed by 5 s to ~4 min). About 2,300 jobs and 2,400 datafeeds became unassigned, and publications again took 40–49 s until the jobs reopened.
- ML nodes were idle throughout (about 0 % CPU, 27–35 % ML memory). The 16-open-jobs-per-node limit was reached on every ML node.

1. **Every unassigned datafeed is re-evaluated on every relevant cluster state update, on the applier thread.**
   [`PersistentTasksClusterService.shouldReassignPersistentTasks`](https://github.com/elastic/elasticsearch/blob/v8.19.19/server/src/main/java/org/elasticsearch/persistent/PersistentTasksClusterService.java#L424) runs on any change in nodes, routing table, metadata or persistent tasks. For each task that `needsReassignment`, it calls `createAssignment`, which calls the executor's `getAssignment`. [`reassignTasks`](https://github.com/elastic/elasticsearch/blob/v8.19.19/server/src/main/java/org/elasticsearch/persistent/PersistentTasksClusterService.java#L463) then repeats the same loop on the master service thread. An unassigned task stays in this set until it is assigned, so the cost per update is proportional to the number of unassigned tasks.

2. **The expensive check runs before the cheap one.**
   [`DatafeedNodeSelector.checkAssignment`](https://github.com/elastic/elasticsearch/blob/v8.19.19/x-pack/plugin/ml/src/main/java/org/elasticsearch/xpack/ml/datafeed/DatafeedNodeSelector.java#L137) calls `verifyIndicesActive()` first (line 139), and only afterwards checks the job state and `isStatusStale` (line 162). `verifyIndicesActive()` resolves the datafeed's index expressions with `resolver.concreteIndexNames(...)` ([line 181](https://github.com/elastic/elasticsearch/blob/v8.19.19/x-pack/plugin/ml/src/main/java/org/elasticsearch/xpack/ml/datafeed/DatafeedNodeSelector.java#L181)) and then checks the routing table of every resolved index. In the incident, ~1,545 datafeeds were evaluated while their job state was stale, so the result of the index check could not change the outcome. Measured cost is about 8 ms per datafeed per pass, which means tens of seconds per update with 2,000+ unassigned datafeeds.

3. **Possible extra cost for remote-only datafeeds (to be confirmed by the reproduction below).**
   `verifyIndicesActive()` removes remote index expressions before resolving, so a datafeed that only reads remote indices passes an empty array to `concreteIndexNames`. By reading [`resolveExpressionsToResources`](https://github.com/elastic/elasticsearch/blob/v8.19.19/server/src/main/java/org/elasticsearch/cluster/metadata/IndexNameExpressionResolver.java#L305), an empty expression list with wildcard expansion enabled (the datafeed default `expand_wildcards: open`) resolves to all indices. If that is right, every remote-only datafeed resolves and checks all ~14k local indices on every pass. About half of the datafeeds on this cluster are remote-only, so this could be a large share of the cost. I have not yet confirmed this with a test.

4. **Every ML task-state write is its own cluster state update.**
   [`updatePersistentTaskState`](https://github.com/elastic/elasticsearch/blob/v8.19.19/server/src/main/java/org/elasticsearch/persistent/PersistentTasksClusterService.java#L247) submits an unbatched task per call. Each job reaching `opened` and each datafeed reaching `started` therefore pays one full publication. Because of (1), each of these publications is slow, and each one that leaves tasks unassigned is followed by another full scan. Recovery speed is limited by publications per hour, not by ML node capacity. This probably explains why the ML nodes were idle during recovery.

5. **The job-stats API can hide the state.** `GET _ml/anomaly_detectors/_stats` reports `MlTasks.getJobState`, which does not check `isStatusStale`, so jobs that the master considers stale and unassigned are reported as `opened`. The reliable signal is the datafeed's `assignment_explanation` (`...state is stale`).

- **Snapshot backlog.** The queue was 91 % `update snapshot state` tasks, but queue composition does not show that snapshots caused the problem. Those tasks run in one batch at `NORMAL` priority, and a long queue of them usually means something else holds higher-priority slots on the master. We should not recommend "pause SLM" as a mitigation based on this data alone. It needs to be checked against the master's actual task execution times (for example, `cluster.service` task-execution logging and `GET _cluster/pending_tasks` with priorities, captured over time).
- **`node_concurrent_job_allocations`.** It was 16. Whether a lower value helps is untested. Jobs that cannot be placed stay in the re-evaluation set, so the effect on total recovery time is unknown. Not recommended as a mitigation until tested.
- **Master sizing.** Heap was about 50 % with no old-generation GC, and the hot thread is one applier thread at 100 % of one core. More heap or vCPUs is not expected to help.
- **Unrelated to ML load.** In the second trigger, the node loss started before the reported data-source recovery and on nodes on two allocator hosts, which points to a host or network event. The ML-specific part is only the amplification after the nodes left.

Goal: show the slow publication at a scale similar to the above, with a reproducible measurement.

1. Cluster: 3 dedicated masters, 3–8 ML nodes with enough ML memory for ~3k small jobs, ~14k indices (small, 1 shard, 0 replicas is enough) including a few data streams with 400–1,200 backing indices.
2. ML: create ~3k jobs with real-time datafeeds. Mix: ~50 % datafeeds with only remote index expressions (a second local cluster is enough as the remote), ~50 % with local data stream patterns. Open and start them.
3. Trigger A: `POST _ml/set_upgrade_mode?enabled=true`, wait for all datafeeds to be unassigned, then `enabled=false`.
4. Trigger B: stop several ML nodes at once (or isolate them with a network partition for ~2 minutes) so that ~2k tasks become unassigned.
5. Measure on the elected master: `ClusterApplierService` slow-task warnings, per-listener timing, `GET _nodes/<master>/stats/discovery` (`cluster_state_update.*.master_apply_time_millis`), pending-task queue with priorities, hot threads, and the time until no datafeed has `state is stale`.
6. Run the variants: only local datafeeds, only remote-only datafeeds, and a mix. This separates point 3 above from points 1 and 2.
7. A microbenchmark of `DatafeedNodeSelector.selectNode` with N datafeeds against a cluster state with 14k indices (with and without a remote-only datafeed list) is a cheaper way to test point 3 before a full reproduction.

In rough order of effort. A and B are small, local to ML, and can be backported. C and D change the persistent-task framework.

- **A. Check the cheap conditions first.** In `DatafeedNodeSelector.checkAssignment`, evaluate job state, stale state and upgrade/reset mode before `verifyIndicesActive()`. A datafeed that cannot be assigned because its job is not open does not need the index check. Expected effect: removes most of the cost in the incident above (~1,545 of the evaluated datafeeds had a stale job). Risk: the explanation text returned for a datafeed that fails both checks changes. Check that tests and users do not depend on the current priority order of failures (`PriorityFailureCollector`).
- **B. Do not resolve local indices for remote-only datafeeds.** If point 3 is confirmed, skip the local resolution when the filtered list is empty. A guard of this kind exists on `main` for ES|QL datafeeds with an empty configured list, but it does not cover the remote-only case, as far as I can tell.
- **C. Avoid re-evaluating unchanged inputs.** An unassigned datafeed's assignment depends on its own job's state, node availability, and the routing and metadata of its indices. Options: remember the last result per task and re-evaluate only when the job's task or the datafeed's resolved indices changed; or resolve each distinct index expression once per cluster state and share the result between datafeeds (many datafeeds share the same data streams). Larger change, but it also covers other persistent task types.
- **D. Batch persistent-task state updates.** Move `updatePersistentTaskState` (and possibly create/complete/remove) to a batched `MasterServiceTaskQueue`, so that many ML state transitions in one window cost one publication. This addresses point 4 directly and applies to 9.x as well.
- **E. Throttle or batch the assignment burst.** When upgrade mode is disabled, or many nodes leave at once, assign tasks in limited batches (or with a global cap on tasks assigned per cluster state update) instead of making all tasks assignable together. This reduces the thundering herd but not the per-update cost, so it should come after A–C.
- **F. Improve the diagnostics.** Log which listener and which task type consume the time in a slow persistent-tasks pass, report staleness in `_ml/anomaly_detectors/_stats`, and document how to read `assignment_explanation`.

1. Run the microbenchmark (reproduction step 7) to confirm or reject point 3.
2. Implement A (and B if confirmed) with a unit test that asserts the cheap checks run first and that the resolver is not called for a datafeed with a stale job.
3. Run the full reproduction on a large test cluster, before and after A/B, to get the numbers for recovery time.
4. Decide on C, D and E based on what remains after A/B.
```

```
ThreadPoolMergeScheduler throttles indexing too late to bound segment growth when merges fall behind (heap exhaustion)

### Summary

When merges fall behind on a node, nothing in the current throttling logic reliably bounds how many segments pile up. On a production hot node (9.4.4, 8 vCPU, 7.3 GiB heap, ~300 shards, wide mappings of ~966 fields), the segment count grew from ~3.3K to ~21.9K over about 20 hours. Per-segment reader metadata filled the heap and the JVM exited with OOM. The node then entered a restart loop, since recovery reopens every segment.

  ### What we observed (hot node vs. its two hot-tier peers, same workload)

  - Merge pool (8 threads) saturated for ~20 h: ~14–17K merge-thread-seconds per 30 min, versus ~1.4–5.6K on peers. Average merge duration was 6–10x longer than on peers.
  - Segments: 3.3K -> 21.9K on this node; 3–4.5K and flat on peers. One shard reached 1,004 segments, versus <= ~115 for sibling shards of the same index on other nodes.
  - Old gen: 3.1 -> 7.3 GiB of 7.86 GiB, tracking ~225 KB per segment.
  - When throttling engaged on many shards segments kept growing from ~4K to ~22K over the next ~16 hours. That's because **indexing throttling, when engaged, only restricts indexing to 1 thread.**

  In this case merges slowed down because of IO (a separate issue, tracked elsewhere), but any cause of slow merges (slow disk, noisy neighbours, very large merges) leads to the same failure mode, and the scheduler offers no protection against it.

  ### Why the current logic can be too late

  `ThreadPoolMergeScheduler.checkMergeTaskThrottling` enables indexing throttling for a shard only when **both** hold:
  1. `submitted - done > max_merge_count` (default `max_thread_count + 5`, i.e. 9 with 8 processors). This is per shard, in **merges**, not segments or heap.
  2. `auto_throttle` is off, **or** `ThreadPoolMergeExecutorService.usingMaxTargetIORateBytesPerSec()` is true. The merge IO target starts at 20 MB/s and rises by 20% per submission when the node-wide count of IO-throttled merge tasks exceeds `2 x merge pool size`, so reaching the 10,240 MB/s ceiling takes roughly 35 increases.

  Consequences:
  - The limit is per shard. With ~300 shards, up to ~9 outstanding merges each can sit behind a small merge pool with no node-level backpressure.
  - The limit is expressed in merges. Whether a shard can accumulate hundreds of segments while at or below the limit depends on the merge policy's selection, which I haven't confirmed.
  - Even when active, the throttle limits indexing to one thread per shard (`Engine.IndexThrottle`) rather than stopping it. Segments kept growing for ~16 hours with throttling on.
  - Nothing accounts for the heap cost of segments.

  ### Suggestions for discussion

  1. Trigger throttling earlier when the merge pool is saturated and the backlog is growing, independent of the IO-rate ceiling.
  2. Add **node-level** backpressure, e.g. total outstanding merges versus `k x merge pool size`, applied to the shards contributing most.
  3. Make backpressure segment- or heap-aware, e.g. a per-shard or per-node limit on segment count, or an estimate of reader memory (segments x fields) with indexing backpressure before the heap is exhausted.
  4. Escalate from "one thread per shard" to a complete pause above a higher threshold.

  Throttling indexing earlier has a throughput cost, so any of this probably wants to be configurable.
```

```
Enrich cache returns wrong results for geo_match processors with different shape_relation on the same policy

The enrich processor cache key does not include the geo_match `shape_relation` (or `orientation`). If two `geo_match` enrich processors use the same policy, look up the same input value and have the same `max_matches`, but use different `shape_relation`s, the processor that runs second is served the cached result of the first one instead of running its own query. The document is enriched with the wrong data, and nothing fails or warns.

The defect is in the shared enrich lookup cache (`EnrichCache`, `AbstractEnrichProcessor`, `EnrichProcessorFactory` in `x-pack/plugin/enrich`), not in the geo query itself: `GeoMatchProcessor` builds the correct query, but the cache is consulted with a key that leaves out the per-processor settings that go into that query. Only `geo_match` policies are affected in practice, because they are the only ones with such settings. `:Analytics/Geo` is added for visibility.

Introduced by #120256 ("Improve memory aspects of enrich cache"), which changed the cache key from `(enrichIndex, SearchRequest)` (which included the full query, relation included) to `(enrichIndex, lookupValue, maxMatches)`. That PR was backported, so this affects 8.16.4+, 8.17.2+, 8.18.0+ and all 9.x versions.

Wrong enrichment results, silently. It only happens when, within the cache lifetime (on the same node), more than one `geo_match` enrich processor:
- references the same enrich policy (and so the same concrete `.enrich-*` index), and
- looks up an equal input value with the same `max_matches`, and
- uses a different `shape_relation` (`intersects` / `disjoint` / `within` / `contains`) or a different `orientation`.

These processors may be in the same pipeline or in different pipelines. Whichever processor caches first decides the result for all the others until the entry is evicted or the policy is re-executed. `match` and `range` policies are not affected: their query depends only on the enrich index (match field from `_meta`) and the lookup value.

    POST users/_doc
    { "location": "POLYGON((-122.08592534065245 37.38501746624134, -122.08193421363829 37.38501746624134, -122.08193421363829 37.3879329075567, -122.08592534065245 37.3879329075567, -122.08592534065245 37.38501746624134))", "zipcode": "94040" }
    POST users/_doc
    { "location": "POLYGON((-74.01 40.70, -73.99 40.70, -73.99 40.72, -74.01 40.72, -74.01 40.70))", "zipcode": "10004" }
    POST users/_refresh

    PUT _enrich/policy/my-policy
    { "geo_match": { "indices": "users", "match_field": "location", "enrich_fields": ["zipcode"] } }
    POST _enrich/policy/my-policy/_execute

    PUT _ingest/pipeline/my-pipeline
    {
      "processors": [
        { "enrich": { "policy_name": "my-policy", "field": "location", "target_field": "intersects", "shape_relation": "intersects", "max_matches": 1 } },
        { "enrich": { "policy_name": "my-policy", "field": "location", "target_field": "disjoint", "shape_relation": "disjoint", "max_matches": 1 } }
      ]
    }

    PUT my-index/_doc/1?pipeline=my-pipeline
    { "location": "37.386444, -122.083863" }

Expected: `intersects.zipcode == "94040"`, `disjoint.zipcode == "10004"`.
Actual: `disjoint.zipcode == "94040"`. The second processor reuses the first one's cached hits, and enrich stats show a single executed search.

- `EnrichCache.java:105` / `:185`: `CacheKey(projectId, enrichIndex, lookupValue, maxMatches)`.
- `AbstractEnrichProcessor.java:87` passes the raw document field `value` as the lookup value. `EnrichProcessorFactory.java:144-148` forwards it to `EnrichCache#computeIfAbsent`. The actual query is built lazily inside the fetcher (`EnrichProcessorFactory.java:151`) and never becomes part of the key.
- `GeoMatchProcessor.java:43-45` builds `new GeoShapeQueryBuilder(matchField, parser.parseGeometry(value)).relation(shapeRelation)`. Here `shapeRelation` and `orientation` (the latter used to build the `GeometryParser`, `GeoMatchProcessor.java:38`) are per-processor settings (`EnrichProcessorFactory.java:111-114`) that change the search but are not in the key.
```

```
Data stream mapping APIs validate with the write index settings, not the template settings

The data stream mapping and settings APIs check the effective mappings (template mappings plus data stream mapping overrides) in a temporary index. That temporary index uses the settings of the current write index, not the settings of the template. The next write index is created from the template. So if a template changes a setting that mapping validation reads, these APIs reject mappings that a rollover accepts.

The javadoc of `DataStream#getEffectiveMappings` says it returns "the mappings that would be used to create the write index if this data stream were rolled over right now". With these steps, the rollover succeeds, but this method fails.

We reproduced it on `main` (commit `b7d133b46510`) with two settings:
- `index.mapping.total_fields.limit`
- a custom analyzer in `index.analysis`

We did not test other settings that mapping validation reads, for example `index.mapping.depth.limit` or `index.mapping.nested_fields.limit`.

1. Create a template with `data_stream: {}` and `index.mapping.total_fields.limit: 2`, with the fields `@timestamp` and `a`. Create a data stream.
2. Update the template to `index.mapping.total_fields.limit: 5`, with 4 fields. Do not change `index.mode`. The template saves.
3. Call `GET _data_stream/<name>/_mappings`, `GET _data_stream/<name>/_settings`, and `PUT _data_stream/<name>/_mappings`.
4. Roll over the data stream.

Actual result:
- Both GET calls return HTTP 400: `Failed to parse mapping: Limit of total fields [2] has been exceeded`.
- `PUT _data_stream/<name>/_mappings` returns HTTP 200 with `applied_to_data_stream: false` and the error `Failed to parse mapping: Limit of total fields [2] has been exceeded`.
- The rollover succeeds. The new write index accepts the same mappings.

With a custom analyzer that only the updated template defines, `GET _data_stream/<name>/_mappings` returns HTTP 400: `Failed to parse mapping: analyzer [my_analyzer] has not been configured in mappings`. The rollover succeeds.

Expected result: the APIs check the mappings with the settings that the next write index gets, so all calls succeed.

The error stays until the next rollover.

`DataStream.getEffectiveMappings` passes `projectMetadata.index(writeIndex)` to `IndicesService.withTempIndexService`, and then merges the template mappings into that temporary index. The merge reads limits and analyzers from the write index settings.

#164441 (case 1) has the same cause for `index.mode`. The fix for #164441 builds the temporary index from the template settings only when the template `index.mode` differs from the write index. This issue is about the case where the mode is the same.

Build the temporary index from the resolved template settings (`MetadataIndexTemplateService.resolveSettings`), as rollover does. Some things to check:
- Index setting providers add settings at index creation, for example the routing path of `time_series` indices. The temporary index does not have them.
- The index version changes from the version of the write index to the current version.
```

```
Uncharged per-clause bit sets can OOM a node

main

_bundled_

Query cache population is now charged to the request circuit breaker (#165667), and so is scoring for `PointRangeQuery` and costly `MultiTermQuery`s (`ContextIndexSearcher#chargingExecutionMemory`). Several other queries and aggregations still build a `FixedBitSet`/`LongBitSet` of `maxDoc` (or of the field's ordinal count) for each clause, without telling any breaker. A single `bool` with a few thousand such clauses, which is under the default clause limit, or a few thousand aggregations, can then exhaust the heap.

Points/shape queries are not charged in `ContextIndexSearcher#chargingExecutionMemory`. Their scorers are built all at once for a disjunction, so every clause's bit set is alive at the same time.

Searches on a plain `IndexSearcher`, which bypasses all charging:

Aggregation-time bit sets:

Strict columnar: include_in_parent/include_in_root fails on binary doc values fields

In a strict columnar index, a `nested` object with `include_in_parent` or `include_in_root` fails to index once two or more nested objects hold a value for the same `keyword`, `text`, `ip` or `binary` field:

```
IllegalArgumentException: DocValuesField "n.f" appears more than once in this document (only one value is allowed per field)
```

`long` fields will have the same problem once #165669 merges, if `index.binary_numeric_doc_values.enabled` is on.

For example:

```
PUT test
{
  "settings": { "index.mode": "columnar" },
  "mappings": {
    "properties": {
      "@timestamp": { "type": "date" },
      "n": { "type": "nested", "include_in_parent": true, "properties": { "f": { "type": "keyword" } } }
    }
  }
}
[... 3 more lines]
```

The same mapping indexes fine with `SORTED_SET` / `SORTED_NUMERIC` doc values.

In strict columnar mode these fields write binary doc values. Each document gets one keyed field holding all of that document's values, built through `LuceneDocument#getOrAddWithKey` (`ColumnarBinaryDocValuesField`, `MultiValuedBinaryDocValuesField`, `ColumnarNumericDocValuesField`). Each nested object is its own Lucene document, so each one holds its own payload. `DocumentParser#copyNestedFields` then copies every field of the nested document into the parent or root with a plain `add`. With two nested objects the parent ends up with two binary doc values fields of the same name, which Lucene rejects. With one nested object the parent holds a single copy, so it indexes fine.

#142594 is the same problem for `dense_vector`.

Either merge a copied payload into the parent's keyed field, or reject `include_in_parent` / `include_in_root` in strict columnar mode.

Merging keeps behaviour the same as sorted doc values, but `copyNestedFields` has to know how to combine each payload format.

ES|QL: Deduplicate aggregations above RERANK and FUSE (low priority)

Follow-up of #166045. This is a corner case and low priority: it is a missed optimization only, the results are correct.

#166045 fixed wrong results from deduplicating aggregations over columns whose values changed in earlier commands. To do that, `ReplaceAggregateAggExpressionWithEval` now only resolves aliases while walking down through plans that keep their input's values, and stops at any plan that writes a new value under one of its input's attributes. As a result, `RERANK` and `FUSE` stop the walk, and two identical aggregations over equal columns defined below them are no longer combined into one, as they were before #166045.

`RERANK` writes its score into the existing `_score`:

```
from test metadata _score
| eval a = salary * 2, b = salary * 2
| rerank "query" on first_name with { "inference_id" : "reranking-inference-id" }
| stats x = min(a), y = min(b), z = max(_score)
```

`FUSE` expands into an aggregate above a `FuseScoreEval`, which rewrites `_score` in place and is not `DocPreserving`:

```
from test metadata _id, _index, _score
| fork (where emp_no > 1 | limit 10) (where emp_no < 5 | limit 10)
| eval a = salary * 2, b = salary * 2
| fuse linear
| keep a, b, _score
```

In both, `MIN(a)`/`MIN(b)` (or the `FIRST` aggregations `FUSE` generates) are computed twice.

Possible approach: instead of stopping at a plan that overwrites an input attribute, keep walking, and skip only the aliases that read or redefine an overwritten attribute. `FuseScoreEval` would also need to declare that it keeps every value except `_score`.

Reported by @fang-xing-esql in https://github.com/elastic/elasticsearch/pull/166045#discussion_r4605650788.

[Transform] Destination index creation overrides `number_of_shards` from matching index templates, breaking Fleet `destination_index_template`

When a transform creates its destination index, the create request carries `number_of_shards: 1` and `auto_expand_replicas: 0-1` from ([DefaultTransformExtension](https://github.com/elastic/elasticsearch/blob/main/x-pack/plugin/transform/src/main/java/org/elasticsearch/xpack/transform/DefaultTransformExtension.java#L28-L38)). Request settings take precedence over template settings, so an index template that matches the destination index cannot set the shard count.

This breaks a feature that integration packages rely on. A package transform can ship a `destination_index_template`, which Fleet installs as an index template (priority 250) composed of a `@package` component template and user-editable `@custom` component templates. Any `number_of_shards` in those templates is ignored when the transform creates the index. Package authors cannot ship a larger default, and users who follow the documented `@custom` pattern get no error or warning that their setting was dropped.

Destination indices of `latest` transforms are single indices that cannot roll over, so the shard count at creation is the only lever for keeping shard size within the recommended range. A single-shard destination index of 76 GB has been reported for one integration.

Observed with the Wiz integration 4.8.0, whose `latest_cdr_vulnerabilities` transform is `unattended` and ships:

```
destination_index_template:
  settings:
    index:
      number_of_shards: 3
```

1. Install or upgrade to Wiz 4.8.0 with vulnerability data present.
2. The component template `logs-wiz.latest_cdr_vulnerabilities-template@package` contains `"number_of_shards": "3"`.
3. `GET security_solution-wiz.vulnerability_latest-v3/_settings` returns:

```
"mapping": { "total_fields": { "limit": "1000" }, "ignore_malformed": "true" },
"number_of_shards": "1",
"auto_expand_replicas": "0-1"
```

The `mapping` settings come from the Fleet templates, so the templates matched. Only the two hardcoded settings were replaced.

- First run of an unattended transform (checkpoint 0): `TransformIndexer` calls `doMaybeCreateDestIndex`, which reaches `TransformIndex.createDestinationIndex` with the hardcoded settings. Result: 1 shard.
- `_start` of a transform that is not unattended: `TransportStartTransformAction` calls the same method with the same settings. Result: 1 shard.
- Destination index missing while the checkpoint is above 0 (for example after stop, delete index, start): the transform skips its own create and the first bulk write auto-creates the index. Result: templates apply.

The same transform therefore gets a different shard count depending on whether it or the bulk request creates the index. The auto-create path also skips `setUpDestinationAliases`, so `dest.aliases` are not re-created there.

- Do not send `index.number_of_shards` on the destination index create request. The default is already 1 when no template sets it, so behavior is unchanged for transforms without a matching template.
- Send `index.auto_expand_replicas: 0-1` only when no matching template sets `auto_expand_replicas` or `number_of_replicas`.

An alternative is to make destination index settings configurable on the transform (for example under `dest`), with the hardcoded values as defaults.

- https://github.com/elastic/elasticsearch/issues/118512 requests the same behavior for user-created transforms.
- https://github.com/elastic/integrations/issues/22309 is the user report for the Wiz integration.
- https://github.com/elastic/integrations/issues/20820 and https://github.com/elastic/integrations/pull/21016 added the 3-shard `destination_index_template` to Wiz; it has no effect on install or upgrade because of this behavior.
```
